analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal offshore waters to oil and gas drilling and shares the royalty money with coastal states.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 232-187, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have revoked federal protections that kept much of the outer Continental Shelf off-limits to drilling, requiring lease sales on at least 75% of unleased acreage in each offshore planning area and opening waters 50 to 100 miles off the Atlantic, Pacific, and eastern Gulf coasts unless a state petitioned in time to keep them closed. It would have handed coastal states a large share of federal offshore drilling revenue — up to roughly two-thirds in near-shore areas — to spend on nearly anything, from college tuition to tax cuts, with no federal accounting. It also cut environmental reviews for offshore drilling and gave producers royalty relief and new lease flexibility. [S3][S4][S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas producers gain the most: new leasing areas 50 to 100 miles from shore, mandated lease sales covering 75% of unleased acreage, streamlined environmental reviews, and price-threshold royalty relief on older Gulf of Mexico leases [S3][S4][S5]. Gulf Coast and other producing states and their coastal local governments would receive up to 42.5% (and up to 63.75% in near-shore zones) of federal offshore receipts, usable for any purpose under state law [S5]. Petroleum and mining engineering schools and scholarship students also gain dedicated funding [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Revokes the 1998 presidential withdrawal and requires the Interior Department to offer leasing in offshore areas between 50 and 100 miles of the Atlantic, Pacific, and eastern Gulf coasts unless an adjacent state petitions in time to keep them closed [S3][S4].
Requires each five-year offshore leasing program to offer at least 75% of the available unleased acreage in every planning area for oil and gas leasing [S3].

Shares federal offshore drilling receipts with adjacent states and coastal local governments — phasing up to 42.5% for most tracts and up to 63.75% within 4 marine leagues of shore — usable for college tuition, transportation, tax cuts, restoration, or any purpose under state law, with no federal accounting required [S5].

Grants categorical exclusions from environmental reviews for seismic surveys and preliminary activities, exempts exploration plans from impact statements, and limits development plans to one full environmental impact statement per decade [S3].

Requires the Interior Secretary to amend 1998-99 Central and Western Gulf leases to add royalty suspension price thresholds ($40.50 per barrel for oil), reducing royalty payments on those leases when prices exceed the thresholds [S5].

Funds petroleum and mining engineering programs at state schools, scholarships including for minority-serving institutions, and grants for geothermal, ocean-energy, coal-to-liquids, oil shale, and other unconventional fuel projects [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and so all taxpayers — would give up the shared share of offshore royalty and bonus-bid revenue, which the bill redirects to coastal states and local governments [S5]. Coastal communities and the public bear the added spill and environmental risk of new drilling closer to shore, with weakened environmental review before leases, exploration, and development [S3]. The bill also bars federal agencies from permitting offshore uses incompatible with oil and gas production, shrinking room for other ocean interests [S3].

drawbacks.text: It strips most environmental review from offshore drilling: seismic surveys and lease suspensions are categorically excluded from environmental assessments, exploration plans need no impact statement, and each planning area gets at most one full environmental review per 10 years [S3].
States receiving shared offshore revenue are not required to account to the federal government for how they spend it, and the allowable uses include reducing state taxes [S5].

It locks in royalty relief: producers on 1998-99 Gulf leases get mandatory royalty suspension thresholds, and new leases carry $9-per-barrel fees only for deepwater leases already paying no royalty above the same price thresholds — a partial fix to a well-known royalty give-away, not a full recovery of the revenue [S5].

States must act on fixed deadlines to keep waters closed — failing to petition within one year for gas or by June 30, 2009 for oil and gas means the areas between 50 and 100 miles offshore are automatically offered for lease [S4].
The bill repeals the coastal impact assistance program and the Energy Policy Act requirement for a comprehensive inventory of offshore oil and gas resources [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The revenue-sharing is a genuine, large benefit for producing and adjacent coastal states — money that can fund tuition, roads, and restoration. But the bill's center of gravity is expanded drilling access with sharply reduced environmental review, mandatory leasing quotas, and royalty relief for producers. The public's side of the trade — a share of revenue routed to a few states, plus royalties forgone from the Treasury — is outweighed by new drilling exposure near coasts and thinner review safeguards, and the no-accounting rule for state spending of federal money is a real design flaw.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 232-187 in June 2006, but the Senate never voted on it — it sat on the Senate calendar until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Jindal introduced the bill on February 15, 2006 with 114 cosponsors (99 Republicans, 15 Democrats) [S1][S6].
The House Natural Resources Committee reported it amended by a 29-9 vote on June 21, 2006 [S7].
The House passed the bill on June 29, 2006 by 232-187: 192 of 230 Republicans voted yes, while only 40 of 201 Democrats did; 155 Democrats, 31 Republicans, and the one Independent voted no [S8][S7].
The Senate received the bill on July 10, 2006 and placed it on the calendar under General Orders on September 5; no vote ever occurred before the Congress ended [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, existing limits on Atlantic, Pacific, and eastern Gulf drilling stayed in place. The coastal communities, fishing and tourism economies, and environmental advocates who opposed new offshore drilling kept the status quo; offshore producers gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal drilling opponents; producers gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party: 192 of 230 Republicans voted yes versus 40 of 201 Democrats, with 155 Democrats, 31 Republicans, and the chamber's one Independent opposed; the Senate never voted.

industries.note: The bill opens 50-100 mile offshore zones to leasing, mandates lease sales on 75% of unleased acreage, curtails environmental review, and adds royalty relief and lease-exchange options for existing California and Florida leaseholders. Producers gain acreage and lower costs; the offsetting public benefits are indirect, while spill risk and forgone federal revenue are direct. [S3][S4][S5]

industries.industry: Coastal state and local governments (producing and adjacent states)
industries.note: States and coastal local governments would receive 42.5% to 63.75% of offshore drilling receipts to spend on tuition, transportation, restoration, or anything state law allows, with no federal accounting. This is a genuine fiscal gain for those communities, funded by redirecting federal revenue. [S5]

industries.industry: Coastal tourism, fishing, and other near-shore ocean users
industries.note: New leasing closer to shore plus categorical exclusions from environmental review reduce the scrutiny that protects fisheries, reefs, and beaches these industries depend on, and the bill bars offshore uses incompatible with oil and gas production. [S3][S4]
The bill directs dedicated federal funding to state-chartered petroleum and mining engineering programs and creates scholarships, including for minority-serving institutions. [S3]
